# Azhi

*The Dragon Philosopher*

Far into the black reaches of time and space, before the known planets were young, is the philosopher dragon Azhi who, even then, is old beyond remembrance. Azhi sails through the galaxy in search of the thing that would make it happy, and for being a philosopher, this is a difficult task; Azhi is hungry, but it knows not for what it hungers.

So it first tastes of the abundant blackness of night, but since the darkness contains nothing at all, it finds this unfulfilling. This puzzles the timeless dragon for an eternity, but soon it resolves, “If consuming nothing gives no happiness, perhaps then it was better to consume something.”

Azhi and its thoughts drift towards a bright point in the sky that is surrounded by a glow of red and green and is so introduced to a star and its nebula. Azhi samples a taste of the star, and finds it rather too spicy and wisely judges against ingesting it whole. It inhales a few fleeting strands of nebula, but the flavour does not linger.

And so it glides through time and space, searching for something to satiate its hunger. It samples pieces of moons, chunks of planets, and eats entire comets whole, but still it does not find what it seeks.

Until one aeon, no different from any other, as it is floating aimlessly between nowhere and nowhere, it comes upon a group of smaller dragons that are, seemingly, playing. The dragons are young, mere hatchlings of thought when compared to the ageless old Azhi. They glide about each other in complex patterns while Azhi observes from a distance pondering this new twist in the universe. The young dragons seem so full of mirth in their play and interaction. Perhaps this was the hunger that bred within.

So Azhi approaches the young dragons, which are of many forms and colours, and introduces itself. “I have come a long way through time and space, devouring much that was to be found, but I have never found the likes of you young dragons. There is much we can teach each other.”

And so Azhi continues onwards through the cosmos, and with it go a band of young dragons. Some prefer the company of speech, and talk with the old philosopher. Others prefer the comfort of play. Two dragons seem the least interested in philosophy, and instead find pleasure simply in flying in great lazy circles around the great Azhi, and Azhi soon discovers that these two dragons have found happiness. As their happiness becomes permanent, their forms become fixed, and the two young dragons turn to gold and to silver, with great wheeling wings and watchful eyes.

Why these creatures would be happy doing the simplest of tasks is beyond the comprehension of the wizened mind of the old, for the gold and silver kindred are elated with living their lives without ever stopping to ponder why they were alive in the first place.

Azhi discusses this with the other dragons, who share speech with Azhi. One dragon becomes Azhi’s greatest pupil, absorbing all the knowledge that he could obtain from the oldest of dragons. And in the blackness of space, this dragon becomes enthralled by knowledge, and takes its final form as a great black wyrm.

The dragons tour the galaxies, stopping at planets and stars to watch as the physics of the universe unfolded. The planets filled with water are ever the favourite of the one dragon, while the frozen wastes are preferred by another. One loves the heat of the molten fires of planets nearly formed. These dragons take forms of Blue, White and Red, and so too are contented, and through the passage of time, they grow more and more asunder of Azhi, who hesitates to linger at the places that they loved, for though he enjoys their company, he does not share in their joy discovered.

Still, some of the young play, and some grow wiser. One dragon turns to Azhi and says, “It is fine that we travel the universe to see what may be, but can we not also create new things?”

Azhi ponders this for an age, thinking that perhaps creation was what it hungered for. It decides that the knowledge of the dragon kindred should be used for creation, and when they encountered a dead planet floating in the bleakness of interstellar space, Azhi instructs them to begin creating a world, though for what purpose, it did not yet know.

The Gold and Silver dragons fly around the barren ball of rock, providing light by which the other dragons could see. The Blue fills the world with water, and the White freezes parts of the world into ice. The Red brings forth great lavas from the deeps of the world and casts them into mountains. And now finally, the last of the young dragons discovers what it was destined to do, for from it springs forth life, hitherto unseen by any of the dragons, and the first fully new creation since Azhi could remember pondering the universe. And so, as life, in a multitude of forms springs forth from the world, the young dragon took upon itself a green colour.

Azhi looks down at the planet in wonder, for it was the most beautiful of the planets it had yet encountered. “What do you have to contribute?” it asks the Black.

The Black ponders for a moment, knowing that all of the other dragons have endowed their loves upon the planet, and said “I will give that which is on the planet knowledge of us, so that we may be worshipped.” And so the life on the planet becomes aware of the dragons, and learns to control fire, water, earth and ice. For a while, they grow together in harmony.

But Azhi speaks of his hunger that still lingers, even now that it has the company of others and has known the joy of creation. It soon grows weary of the other dragons’ youth and especially of their happiness that Azhi does not share.

And so it was that Azhi thinks back to the time of its earliest memories, to when consuming the darkness had failed to satiate. And at that time, Azhi had decided, philosophically, that if the darkness did not cure its hunger, then perhaps it should try the opposite. Thus, by parallel idealism, Azhi now decides that if creation fails to satisfy, then perhaps destruction might.

So Azhi ingests the world.

This upsets and angers the other dragons, who had laboured long and hard in its creation, and had grown in their happiness to greater stature than of that when they were first discovered. They turn to the old philosopher, who had previously only known loneliness and friendship, and they challenge Azhi with a new emotion, that of hatred.

But Azhi is much greater than the young dragons, and is emboldened by this new emotion. Azhi eats them too.

And then there is nothing again, just Azhi and the cosmos, for though all of life had but a brief chance to exist, it had been devoured in its entirety leaving the dragon philosopher alone once again with its thoughts.

Then Azhi fights with its thoughts, for there seemed nothing that could still the hunger within, and it never could find something to make it happy. And the philosopher contemplates for the first time death, for if there was nothing for which to live, there was no reason to live. And so it is that Azhi decides to eat itself, for it had sampled the rest of the known cosmos and not found happiness.

But Azhi is tremendously long, and had grown considerably through all it had ingested. As it samples its tail, it pulls itself into a large loop in the blackness of space. And so it is, that as Azhi pierces its own hide and feels pain for the first time, out of the wounds flow not blood but all that Azhi had consumed. And still it continues to eat, pulling itself into a tighter and tighter loop, while oceans and glaciers and mountains and forests flow forth from its wounds, and soon too, the seven young dragons are freed from their prisons within and all life springs forth anew. But still Azhi continues to eat, until the very spine of its body is bound so tightly into a ring that it cannot contract itself any further.

And so it is that Azhi dies, and never knows happiness.
